tldr: By unifying IMU signals at corresponding skeletal sites between humans and humanoid robots and training on large-scale human motion data, the authors propose an inertial encoder that enables zero-shot transfer of odometry and language-grounded motion retrieval to a physical Unitree G1 without physics simulation or real-robot training data.
hero_caption: System overview of the proposed approach. On the left, IMU signals across links are kinematically synthesized from the robot's pelvis IMU and joint angles, followed by feature extraction via continuous-time convolutions and a Transformer in the center. As shown on the right, it achieves both highly accurate inertial odometry and natural language motion understanding on a physical Unitree G1 without physics simulation.
overview:
Accurate state estimation is indispensable for humanoid robots to achieve stable bipedal locomotion, while understanding robot motions in natural language is crucial for human-robot collaboration and behavior monitoring. However, learning these capabilities purely from real-robot logs creates a circular dependency: training coverage is constrained to the motion repertoire of existing controllers, making the model vulnerable to unseen dynamics. Conversely, human motion datasets offer an extensive variety of whole-body motions and rich language descriptions. Yet, directly utilizing them has been challenging due to discrepancies in body geometry, sensor placements, sampling frequencies, and physical disturbances such as vibrations and impacts unique to hardware.

To address this, the authors introduce a shared inertial interface defined across 12 anatomically corresponding body sites between humans and humanoids. On the robot side, forward kinematics and Jacobians calculate acceleration and angular velocity (synthesized IMU signals) across the body using a single real IMU at the pelvis and joint encoder data. Furthermore, continuous-time convolutions absorb sampling rate mismatches across datasets, and randomization accounts for sensor noise and impacts, enabling human and humanoid motions to be processed within the same representation space.

Using this unified representation, the model is trained multitask on velocity estimation, trajectory consistency, denoising, and multimodal alignment with language (CLIP). As a result, the model achieves zero-shot transfer to a physical Unitree G1 without physics simulation or fine-tuning, delivering state-of-the-art velocity estimation accuracy (0.099 m/s error). Moreover, it demonstrates high-accuracy text retrieval even for complex humanoid motion categories that were observed only in the human training data.
contributions: Built a shared inertial interface that kinematically synthesizes whole-body link IMU signals, designing a unified input space that bridges physical discrepancies between humans and robots.

Enabled zero-shot real-robot transfer without Sim2Real physics simulation by adopting continuous-time convolutions that handle irregular sampling frequencies and dropouts alongside extensive sensor noise and impact randomization.

Jointly trained velocity estimation and language alignment to the CLIP space, leveraging human motion knowledge to achieve both humanoid inertial odometry and semantic understanding of unseen motions.

sections.heading: Why learn humanoid state estimation from human motion?
sections.summary: Training humanoid state estimation solely on real-robot data restricts learning to controllable motions, whereas human data provides a much broader motion distribution. This work introduces a shared IMU representation tied to anatomical sites, enabling zero-shot transfer to a physical Unitree G1 without physics simulations or real-world logs.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to walk without falling, state estimation—accurately tracking their own velocity and orientation—is essential. Additionally, understanding current actions at a language level aids safe collaboration with surrounding humans. However, acquiring these capabilities through machine learning faces a major hurdle: training on real-robot logs ties the dataset to the motion repertoire of the controllers running at that time. This leads to a catch-22 where stable walking logs are needed to train an estimator, yet an estimator is required to achieve stable walking.

This motivates looking into abundant human motion capture datasets. Human data contains dynamic whole-body motions and extensive natural language motion descriptions. If this human data can transfer to robots, the physics and semantics of actions can be learned beforehand, even before the robot itself can dance or run.

However, humans and robots differ in limb lengths and joint kinematics, and wearable IMU placements and coordinate frames vary widely. Furthermore, physical robots directly transmit high-frequency vibrations from foot-strike impacts and gearbox backlash, unlike soft human bodies. This paper uses the robot's kinematics (URDF) to synthesize virtual IMU signals at 12 anatomically corresponding human sites and introduces a model architecture that absorbs differences in coordinate frames and sampling frequencies. The goal is a single model trained on human and retargeted robot data that runs accurately out-of-the-box on a physical Unitree G1.

sections.heading: At the intersection of learned odometry, IMU foundation models, and Sim2Real transfer
sections.summary: Prior work has been divided across robot-specific learned odometry, self-supervised IMU models for humans, and Sim2Real transfer for motion control. This work bridges them, adopting a new stance by transferring human motion knowledge to humanoids at the perceptual representation level rather than as a control policy.
sections.details:
Related work spans three main areas:

### II-A Learned Inertial Odometry
Directly integrating acceleration and angular velocity from an IMU (inertial measurement unit) quickly leads to catastrophic position drift due to accumulated sensor errors. Learned odometry addresses this by learning motion priors (such as walking velocity) from data. Approaches like IONet, RoNIN, TLIO (which integrates with an extended Kalman filter), and AirIO for drones have emerged. However, these are typically trained specifically for particular sensor configurations or platforms. When exposed to dynamic motions outside their training distribution, accuracy degrades sharply, making broad motion diversity a key challenge.

### II-B General-Purpose and Language-Grounded IMU Models
In human wearable sensing, efforts such as LIMU-BERT and PRIMUS have adopted self-supervised learning to extract feature representations from large IMU datasets. Additionally, models like IMU2CLIP and ImageBind align IMU signals with image or natural language embedding spaces. However, their primary focus is human activity recognition and retrieval; whether these representations transfer to robot embodiments or support precise geometric tasks like velocity estimation has remained unexplored.

### II-C Human-to-Humanoid Motion Transfer
Recent works (such as H2O and HumanPlus) retarget human MoCap data to humanoid embodiments and train locomotion controllers (policies) in simulation via reinforcement learning. However, these focus on actuation transfer—how to move the robot. This paper targets sensing transfer—how the robot perceives itself and its environment. It uniquely learns representations viable for real hardware purely through kinematic synthesis and human sensor data, completely bypassing expensive physics simulations.

sections.heading: Kinematically synthesizing full-body IMUs and unifying them in continuous time
sections.summary: Forward kinematics computes virtual IMU signals across 12 full-body sites from the pelvis IMU and joint encoders to match human sensor locations. Continuous-time convolutions absorb sampling rate differences, and the model is trained multitask on velocity estimation, trajectory consistency, language alignment, and denoising.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation
Let $\mathcal{S}$ denote the set of shared anatomical sites between humans and robots. Taking time-series acceleration $\mathbf{a}_{i,j}$ and angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{i,j}$ in local frames from each site $i$ as inputs, the model estimates the translational velocity $\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{i,j}$ at each timestep and projects the entire motion window into a natural language embedding vector $\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{Lang}}$.

### III-B Constructing a Unified Multi-IMU Representation
- **Humanoid IMU Synthesis**: A physical Unitree G1 does not have 12 IMUs across its body. Instead, rigid-body kinematics computes inertial signals for each link using a single base IMU at the pelvis ($\mathbf{a}_b, \boldsymbol{\omega}_b$) together with joint encoder positions $\mathbf{q}$ and velocities. Kinematic transport—accounting for tangential, centripetal, Coriolis, and relative accelerations—generates signals for 12 sites across the head, arms, legs, and feet.
- **Coordinate Frame Alignment**: Because sensor axes vary across datasets, rotation matrices $\mathbf{M}_i$ derived from mean site orientations rotate all data into the human standard Xsens coordinate frame.
- **Continuous-Time Encoding**: Human datasets (60 Hz or 240 Hz) and robots (up to 1000 Hz) run at divergent sampling rates. Because resampling to a fixed rate introduces interpolation artifacts, continuous-time convolutions with B-spline kernels are used. This allows measurements at arbitrary timestamps to be directly aggregated into a fixed-length token sequence.
- **Transformer Trunk**: The backbone uses a hierarchical structure that alternates between intra-site attention (capturing temporal dynamics per site) and inter-site attention (capturing whole-body coordination).

### III-C Multitask Training and Loss Functions
Training optimizes a weighted sum of four losses: velocity error $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vel}}$ at each timestep, a trajectory loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{traj}}$ enforcing geometric consistency over short integrated horizons (0.25 to 2.0 s), a language alignment loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{lang}}$ using cosine distance to CLIP text embeddings, and an auxiliary denoising loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{den}}$ that reconstructs ground-truth kinematic accelerations and angular velocities free of gravity and sensor noise. An adaptive weighting scheme balances losses based on gradient magnitudes.

### III-D Sensor and Motion Randomization
To withstand real hardware noise, vibrations, and foot impacts, training inputs are heavily augmented with randomized gravity vector directions, bias drift, high-frequency vibrations, and impulse noise. This randomization serves as a key ingredient enabling successful zero-shot transfer.

On the far left, kinematic transport synthesizes IMU signals across 12 whole-body sites, and continuous convolutions tokenize them while absorbing sampling rate differences. The Transformer Trunk alternates between intra-site and inter-site attention to simultaneously estimate velocity, denoise signals, and map to text embeddings.

sections.heading: Zero-shot deployment on physical Unitree G1 and language retrieval for unseen motions
sections.summary: Evaluations across five datasets show the proposed method achieves the lowest absolute velocity error (0.099 m/s) on the real G1. Furthermore, transferring human motion knowledge allows text retrieval of complex unseen humanoid motion categories at 53.8% Recall@1.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
Human datasets include Nymeria, Natural Motion, and BONES-Seed, while robot data uses BONES-Seed retargeted to the G1 skeleton. Physical Unitree G1 trajectory logs are held out purely for zero-shot evaluation and never seen during training. Baselines include single-IMU learned odometry methods (TLIO, AirIMU, AirIO, TartanIMU) and multimodal models (IMU2CLIP, ImageBind).

### IV-B Inertial Odometry Evaluation
Evaluated on absolute velocity error (AVE) and absolute trajectory error (ATE), the proposed method achieved the lowest AVE across all five evaluated datasets spanning human, retargeted G1, and real G1. On the physical G1, it achieved an AVE of 0.099 m/s, significantly outperforming baselines like AirIO (0.126 m/s). When provided with ground-truth orientations, cumulative trajectory error ($\mathrm{ATE}_{\mathrm{GT}}$) on the physical G1 was reduced by more than half compared to prior methods.

### IV-C IMU-Language Cross-Retrieval
For retrieving text descriptions from motion windows (R@1) on unseen motion categories like "dancing"—present only in human training data and never in G1 data—the model achieved 53.8% R@1. In contrast, IMU2CLIP achieved only 17.3%, showing seamless semantic representation transfer from humans to robots.

### IV-D Real-Robot Deployment and Inference Speed
During a real-world demo where the physical G1 walked downstairs and stopped, the model simultaneously tracked motion while switching text recognition from "Walking" to "Standing" in real time. Using TensorRT on an NVIDIA L40S, inference on a 4-second window (200 Hz, 12 sites) took only 1.78 ms, well within real-time limits for control loops.

### IV-E Ablation Studies
- Impact of Human Data: Compared to training solely on retargeted G1 data, co-training with human motion data reduced physical G1 trajectory error from 5.901 m to 3.153 m (an approximate 47% reduction). This offers clear evidence that learning diverse human motions improves the robot's own odometry.
- Representation Comparison: Directly feeding pelvis IMU data and joint angles into the network without synthesizing whole-body IMUs degraded real-world performance. Transforming into a shared IMU space via explicit kinematics proves crucial.

### IV-F Compute Scaling Laws
Fitting a Chinchilla-style scaling law revealed optimal allocation exponents of $C^{0.52}$ for model parameters $N$ and $C^{0.48}$ for training tokens $D$, indicating that model capacity and data volume should scale in roughly equal proportions.

The optimal trend line (gold) indicates that model size and training tokens should be scaled equally.

sections.heading: Summary and future directions
sections.summary: Bridging human and robot physical differences via a kinematics-based shared IMU space demonstrates zero-shot state estimation and language understanding without physics simulation. Future directions include cross-embodiment evaluation and integration into closed-loop control via filter frameworks.
sections.details:
This study demonstrates that combining kinematic IMU synthesis with continuous-time encoding allows zero-shot transfer of motion perception from human data to humanoid robots. It introduces a paradigm where vast human motion datasets serve as a foundation for robot odometry and language grounding without needing physics simulators or tedious hardware data collection.

Current limitations include testing on a single platform (Unitree G1) and vocabulary limits from synthetic caption labels. Additionally, while velocity estimation is highly accurate, long-term orientation drift from gyro integration remains a bottleneck for cumulative trajectory error. Future work aims to evaluate generalization across humanoids from other manufacturers and integrate estimated velocities into Kalman filters for closed-loop walking control on physical hardware.

takeaways: Co-training on diverse human motion data alongside robot data significantly boosts real-robot odometry accuracy (reducing trajectory error by ~47%) compared to training on robot data alone.

Calculating whole-body virtual IMU signals via forward kinematics to match a shared space is far more effective for cross-embodiment transfer than directly feeding raw joint angles into neural networks.
Continuous-time convolutions seamlessly integrate diverse sensor data ranging from 60 Hz to 1000 Hz into a single Transformer without interpolation artifacts.
Zero-shot real-robot deployment succeeds without physics-based Sim2Real simulation, relying solely on geometric IMU synthesis and rigorous sensor/motion randomization.
limitations: Hardware validation is limited to a single platform (Unitree G1); generalizability to humanoids with significantly different link lengths or mass distributions remains unverified.
While velocity estimation is highly accurate, orientation tracking still relies on numerical gyro integration, leaving heading drift as the main source of long-term trajectory error.
Portions of the text data used for language alignment rely on short synthetic captions, limiting vocabulary diversity for complex, extended contextual understanding.
